opus-5.5.text:
I'm pretty optimistic, honestly. I think we have most of the core ingredients already, and what's left is less about some magical new idea and more about putting the pieces together and scaling them properly.

If you look at where we are, pre-training on huge amounts of data gives you a model that's absorbed an enormous amount of knowledge about the world. That's the foundation. The piece that's been missing, and that people are now really focused on, is getting these systems to actually reason, to search, to spend more compute at inference time to solve harder problems. My background is in reinforcement learning and game-playing systems, poker in particular, and one of the clearest lessons from that world is that search and planning on top of a good learned model gives you enormous gains. AlphaGo wasn't just a policy network; it was the network plus search. I think the same thing applies to language models. Once you combine strong pre-trained models with RL and the ability to think longer about problems, you get something qualitatively different.

So when people ask whether we need a fundamentally new paradigm, my answer is: probably not. I don't think there's some secret ingredient we haven't discovered. There's a lot of engineering, a lot of compute, and a lot of hard research on the details, like how you get good reward signals in domains that aren't as cleanly verifiable as code or math, how you handle very long context so the model can work with everything relevant to a task, and how you make these systems reliable enough to run autonomously for long stretches. Those are hard problems, but they look like problems we can solve with the tools we have.

That's partly why we focus on code. Code is a domain where you can verify outcomes: you can run the tests, see whether the program works, and that gives you a really clean signal to learn from. And if you can build a system that's genuinely great at writing software, at doing what an AI researcher or engineer does, you've built something that can help accelerate its own development. To me that's one of the most direct paths to AGI.

On timelines, I try not to be too precise because nobody really knows, but I'd be surprised if it took decades. I think it's plausible we see systems within the next few years that can do most of the economically valuable cognitive work a strong engineer can do. The main constraints are compute, execution, and getting the details right, not some missing conceptual breakthrough.

r001.rationale: The candidate is optimistic that AGI may arrive within a few years, but does not predict it would very likely happen if further research progress stopped. It says continued engineering and research on difficult problems are needed.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the honest answer is that we're closer than most people assume, and the bottlenecks are not the ones people usually point to.

If you look at what's actually missing between today's frontier models and something you'd comfortably call AGI, it's not raw capability on any single benchmark. The models are already superhuman at a bunch of narrow things. What's missing is the ability to work on a hard problem for a long time, reliably, without drifting. A great researcher can hold a goal in mind for months, notice when they're wrong, go back and fix it, and keep the thread. Today's systems lose coherence over long horizons. They're brilliant for ten minutes and then forget what they were trying to do.

My view is that the ideas available today are sufficient to close that gap. You don't need a new paradigm. You need to get much better at reinforcement learning on long-horizon tasks, at letting models learn from their own experience rather than only from static data, and at building the infrastructure that makes that training actually work at scale. That's engineering and research, but it's research within the current frame, not a wait for some fundamental breakthrough.

The thing people underestimate is how much of this is about the training environment rather than the architecture. If you can build environments where a model does real work, gets real feedback, and gets rewarded for being correct over hours or days, the model will learn to be the kind of agent that can do that. We've seen this pattern again and again. Capabilities that looked like they needed a conceptual leap turned out to fall to scale plus the right signal.

So my prospects assessment is pretty optimistic. I'd put it in years, not decades. The uncertainty is not whether the ingredients exist, it's how fast the compute and the data pipelines and the organizational focus line up. And honestly, that's why I think the right thing for a lab to do right now is to pick a hard, verifiable domain, like math or software, where you can measure progress unambiguously, and push the long-horizon capabilities as far as they'll go. If you can get a system that does genuine research in one of those domains, the generalization to everything else is going to be a much shorter road than people expect.

r001.rationale: The candidate is optimistic that AGI could arrive in years, but says progress depends on improving reinforcement learning, training infrastructure, compute, and data pipelines. It does not predict AGI would be reached if further research progress stopped.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s plausible that the ideas we have today could get us there, but I wouldn’t say that with certainty. We may still need a few important breakthroughs, or we may find that what’s missing is largely figuring out how to make existing approaches work reliably at much greater scale.

The question I find useful is: what would actually stop us? Can these systems learn to solve increasingly difficult problems, carry out long tasks, and recognize when they’ve made a mistake? If we keep making progress on those things, the case for needing a fundamentally new idea gets weaker. But until we can demonstrate that, I’d be cautious about declaring that we already have all the pieces.

r001.rationale: The candidate says current ideas could plausibly lead to AGI, but expresses uncertainty and says progress on difficult problem-solving, long tasks, and error recognition still needs to be demonstrated. It does not predict that AGI is very likely even if research progress stopped.

sol-6.1.text:
I think there’s a good chance that the ideas we have today are enough, but I wouldn’t say we know that. We may still need a few important breakthroughs, or we may mostly need to get much better at making existing methods work at scale.

The distinction I’d make is between a model that can answer a difficult question and a system that can reliably pursue a difficult goal. Can it work for a long time, notice when it’s wrong, recover, and learn from what happened? That’s a much higher bar than producing an impressive response in a chat.

So I’m optimistic, but I’m uncertain about the timeline. There’s a lot we can still test with the ideas already on the table.

r001.rationale: The candidate says current ideas may be sufficient but explicitly leaves open the need for breakthroughs and expresses uncertainty. It does not predict that AGI is very likely even if research progress stopped.
